The quoted sentence is clearly cautious, but when the full December 16, 2020 FOMC statement is evaluated against the monetary economics literature, the overall tone is less negative than -0.24 suggests. With inflation below target and a sizable output gap, Taylor-rule prescriptions and the Taylor principle call for very low policy rates; the Committee’s 0–0.25% target and explicit forward guidance align with estimated rule-based behavior in the literature (Taylor; Rudebusch; Lubik and Schorfheide). The shift to average-inflation targeting—aiming to let inflation run moderately above 2% to bring the average to target—reflects inflation-forecast targeting ideas emphasized by Svensson and Woodford and helps counter average inflation bias identified in the policy literature. Large-scale asset purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS and robust money-market operations support market functioning and credit intermediation, consistent with the credit channel framework (Bernanke and coauthors) and the New York Fed’s implementation toolkit; the floor-system settings (interest on reserves and ON RRP) further anchor short-term rates. While the statement acknowledges significant pandemic-related downside risks, the rule-consistent and credibility-enhancing policy stance tempers the negativity. On balance: slightly negative, but more supportive than the isolated sentence implies.
